tier_reason: The README Performance section has the exact ops/s table (JS BigInt 256-bit, JS BigInt 128-bit, WASM 128-bit) on an Intel Core i5-7300U, and the harness is public (tests/benchmarks.ts) with build flags in gulpfile.js (asc -O3, AssemblyScript 0.8.1 per package-lock.json). It stays C because the Node.js/V8 version that runs both sides is not stated, the author calls the numbers 'very informal', and the table is a rounded hand conversion that the current script cannot regenerate (it prints milliseconds per 2^18-element pass and its 256-bit section is commented out).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript 0.8.1 (package-lock.json); WASM module built by gulpfile.js with 'npx asc ... --validate --importMemory --enable bulk-memory -O3'; Node.js/V8 version not stated
corrections.caveats: The README calls these 'very informal benchmarks' and gives rounded ops/s figures. The harness is tests/benchmarks.ts (not linked from the README): one Date.now() pass per operation over 2^18-element vectors, with no warm-up or repetition. It prints milliseconds, not the README's ops/s, and its 256-bit JS section is commented out in the current code, so the table cannot be regenerated as-is. The harness checks every WASM result against the JS BigInt result. The Node.js version is unstated and AssemblyScript 0.8.1 is very old. The comparison is against the library's own JS BigInt path only, not C++ or other WASM toolchains. The WASM path covers only moduli 2^128-k with k < 2^64, and WASM memory is never freed (README note). Last commit 2022-05-22.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly (additions 44.0M vs 5.0M vs 3.2M, multiplications 16.3M vs 1.85M vs 0.95M, exponentiations 97,000 vs 10,500 vs 3,200 ops/s); derived ratios of 8.8x, 8.8x and 9.2x over 128-bit BigInt are correct. The README's separate claim that vector, matrix and polynomial ops speed up 6x-10x also appears there. Shortcomings: informal single-pass harness, Node version unstated, baseline is the library's own JS BigInt code, abandoned (last commit 2022-05-22, 43 stars, MIT).

tier_reason: The README's 'WebAssembly support' section has one first-party ratio: slow operations like division are 'around twice as fast' with the wasm.wat module than with the JavaScript fallback. The repo has no benchmark code (tests/ holds unit tests and TypeScript checks; scripts/ only build.js) and no hardware or engine version, so this is a stated ratio without methodology, which is tier C (same as the lodepng 'twice as fast as libpng' precedent).

corrections.caveats: The only evidence is one README phrase ('slow operations like division are around twice as fast'), with no benchmark code in the repo, no hardware, no engine or Node.js version and no operand distribution. The phrase covers division only; multiplication and remainder also use the WASM path (index.js calls wasm mul, div_s/div_u and rem_s/rem_u) but have no stated figure. One WebSearch found no independent measurement; the claim only reappears in README mirrors (forks, @xtuc/long, purescript-int64). The baseline is the library's own JavaScript fallback, not C++ or Emscripten. Fit with assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs is loose: this is a hand-written WAT module (wasm.wat, 213 lines) inside a JavaScript library, not AssemblyScript output. Widely depended on as npm 'long' (for example by protobufjs).

notes: Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 918 stars, 206 forks, not archived or forked, last commit 2025-04-17, so 'stale' is correct. Shortcomings: unmeasured 'around twice as fast' claim for division only, no benchmark code, baseline is the library's own JS fallback, loose category fit. It is notable through npm usage, so it stays listed even though the evidence is thin.

tier_reason: In mathjs discussion #2744 ('Accelerated computations with WASM'), dvd101x posted on 2023-02-11 a single table: mathjs in Safari 2.403 s, mathjs in Chrome 0.475 s, numpy in Pyodide in the browser 0.024 s, native numpy (Python 3.10) 0.009 s, Octave 0.005 s for inv of a random 200x200 matrix. It is an informal third-party post with no machine, browser version, run count or harness, not a peer-reviewed or well-known suite, so it is C.

corrections.caveats: There is one informal timing table from a math.js collaborator (dvd101x, 2023-02-11) in mathjs discussion #2744. It states no machine, OS, browser version, Pyodide version or run count. The poster calls it 'only a quick comparison' and notes that math.js's flexibility adds overhead. Each timed expression includes random-matrix generation (math.random / np.random.rand) as well as the inverse. The win comes from NumPy's compiled LAPACK routines running as WebAssembly against math.js's generic pure-JS matrix code, so it compares implementations more than languages. Native numpy is still about 2.7x faster than numpy in Pyodide (derived from page data). Load and warm-up time are not included. Pyodide publishes no such benchmark; its repo has a benchmark/ directory but no README figures. Fit with assemblyscript-and-wasm-langs is loose: Pyodide is CPython plus scientific packages compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten.

notes: All five numbers in claimed_speedup match the post exactly, and the roughly 20x ratio over math.js in Chrome (0.475/0.024) is correctly marked as derived. Metadata checks out: MPL-2.0, 14.9k stars, last commit 2026-09-22, active. Shortcomings: single informal third-party run with no methodology, generation time included, a LAPACK-vs-pure-JS implementation gap, loose category fit.
